title: Breathless on the hills: exertional dyspnoea and a smoker's cough in a retired teacher
desc: This station is a focused dyspnoea history and respiratory examination of Phoebe Hartley, a 65-year-old retired teacher in general practice. She has months of worsening exertional breathlessness, a chronic cough productive of white sputum, wheeze, frequent chest infections and a 50 pack-year smoking history, and she fears heart failure or lung cancer. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her observations, spirometry, chest X-ray and bloods, diagnoses moderate COPD, explains a management plan to her (smoking, diet and alcohol, physical activity and pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, inhalers with spacer technique), and safety-nets with a written action plan, flare-up signs and follow-up that includes an ECG and cardiovascular risk assessment.
focus: Exertional breathlessness in a heavy smoker: a dyspnoea history that screens cardiac, malignant and interstitial causes, then confirming COPD on spirometry and explaining a COPD-X management plan to the patient
stem: You are a final-year medical student on your general practice placement. Phoebe Hartley is a 65-year-old retired teacher who has come in because she is short of breath when she exerts herself and has a cough bringing up white sputum. Your supervising GP has asked you to see her first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Phoebe and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Phoebe's observations, spirometry, chest X-ray and blood results. Hand over to your supervisor with your interpretation, give your diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Phoebe Hartley, a 65-year-old retired primary school teacher. You are friendly but frustrated. You are comfortable sitting down and speak in full sentences, with an occasional loose cough. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "I just get so breathless these days, and this cough won't go away."

The breathlessness (give only when asked):

  • When: walking, and especially walking uphill.
  • Course: you used to walk for almost an hour every day, hills included, without getting breathless. Over the last few months you get breathless within about a kilometre, and it is slowly getting worse.
  • Recovery: it takes 15 to 20 minutes to settle. Sitting down and resting helps.
  • Impact: "I get breathless extremely easily and it's very frustrating, because I can't finish my usual jobs." You have stopped your daily walks.
  • You are not breathless at rest.

The cough (only if asked): you have had a cough most days for a long time ("a smoker's cough"), worse lately and mainly in the mornings. You bring up white phlegm, about a teaspoon at a time. It has not been green, yellow or brown lately, and you have never coughed up blood.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Wheeze: yes, you hear a whistle in your chest when you are breathless.
  • Chest tightness: yes, a tight feeling across the chest that comes with the breathlessness and wheeze. If asked more: it is not crushing or heavy, does not spread to your arm, neck or jaw, and does not come with sweating or nausea.
  • Tiredness: you feel tired a lot of the time.
  • Chest infections: you had 3 colds in the last year and each one made your breathing much worse for a few weeks. If asked: you saw the GP with the worst one and had a course of antibiotics. You have never been in hospital for your breathing.
  • Negatives, only if asked directly: no weight loss, your appetite is good, no night sweats, no fevers now, no hoarse voice, no lumps in your neck. You sleep on one pillow and can lie flat. You don't wake at night gasping for breath. No ankle swelling, no pink frothy phlegm, no palpitations. No dry tickly cough. No dust, asbestos or chemical exposure (you were a teacher). No recent travel, no contact with anyone with tuberculosis, no one sick around you.

Past medical history: type 2 diabetes for about 8 years and high cholesterol, which is managed with diet. No asthma, now or as a child. You have never had a breathing test or a chest X-ray that you know of.

Medications: metformin and sitagliptin for your diabetes. You don't remember the doses. No puffers. Allergies: none known.

Vaccinations (only if asked): you haven't had a flu shot for a few years and you are not sure about the pneumonia vaccine.

Family history: your mother died of breast cancer at 62. Your younger sister was diagnosed with small cell lung cancer at 40.

Social history:

  • Smoking: you started at 15 and have smoked about a pack (20 cigarettes) a day ever since. (Examiner note: this is 50 pack-years. Do not use the term "pack-years" or do the sum for the candidate.) You chain smoke when you are stressed. If asked: your first cigarette is within 15 minutes of waking. You tried to stop twice, both times cold turkey, and lasted a few weeks each time.
  • Alcohol: 5 to 7 standard drinks on special occasions, otherwise none. No other drugs.
  • Home and support: you live with your husband, and your 2 adult children live nearby. You are well supported. You manage everything at home yourself.
  • Activity: you used to walk every day, but now the breathlessness stops you.
  • Diet: "pretty ordinary". You snack when you are stressed.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are worried that your heart might be failing, or that this might be an early sign of lung cancer like your sister had. You would like to know what is going on and to get something that helps you get back to your walks.

Question to raise: if the candidate has not asked about your worries by the end of the history: "Is this my heart? Or could it be cancer, like my sister?"

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences. Mild pursed-lip breathing after walking into the room. No accessory muscle use at rest. Not cyanosed, not pale. Weight 72 kg, height 163 cm (BMI 27).
  • Vital signs (10:10): HR 88 beats/min regular; BP 136/82 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 94% on room air; temperature 36.7 °C.
  • Hands: nicotine staining of the right index and middle fingers. No clubbing. No flap. Fine tremor absent.
  • Face and neck: no central cyanosis. Trachea midline. JVP not raised. No cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes.
  • Chest: increased front-to-back diameter (barrel-shaped chest). Expansion reduced but symmetrical. Percussion hyper-resonant throughout, with reduced cardiac dullness. Breath sounds reduced throughout, with a prolonged expiratory phase and scattered expiratory wheeze. No crackles (in particular no fine basal crackles). No bronchial breathing, no pleural rub.
  • Cardiovascular: heart sounds dual with no murmur. No ankle or sacral oedema. Calves soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a final-year medical student, confirms Phoebe's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Opens with an open question, uses plain language, acknowledges her frustration and asks about smoking without judgement.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Source marking: 4 marks for the presenting complaint (items 5 to 9 together).

kids.x: Onset and progression: used to walk almost an hour including hills, now breathless within about a kilometre, worsening over the last few months.
kids.d: Credit an exercise tolerance quantified as a distance or time, with the change from before.

kids.x: Triggers and relief: worse walking uphill, takes 15 to 20 minutes to settle, better sitting and resting; not breathless at rest.
Impact: cannot complete her usual tasks and has stopped her daily walks.

check.x: Characterises the cough and sputum: chronic, mainly in the mornings, white sputum; asks about a change to green, yellow or brown (infective flare) and about blood (none).
Asks about associated symptoms and finds wheeze, chest tightness with the breathlessness, and fatigue.
Asks about chest infections and flare-ups: 3 colds in the last year, each making her breathing much worse; one course of antibiotics; no hospital admissions.
Asks about red flags for lung cancer: weight loss, appetite, night sweats, haemoptysis, hoarse voice and lumps (all negative).
Screens for the other causes of breathlessness:
check.d: Source marking: 4 marks for the systems review and the conditions ruled out. Credit each condition screened with at least two relevant questions.

kids.x: Heart failure: orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling, pink frothy sputum (none).
Angina or myocardial infarction: characterises the chest tightness (not crushing, no radiation, no sweating or nausea, comes with wheeze).
Pulmonary fibrosis: dry cough, occupational or dust exposure (none).
Infection or TB: fever, night sweats, travel, TB contact, sick contacts (none).

check.x: Past medical history: type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol; asks about asthma or childhood lung disease and previous breathing tests (none).
Medications (metformin, sitagliptin, no inhalers), allergies (none known) and vaccination status (no recent influenza vaccine, unsure about pneumococcal).
Family history: mother died of breast cancer at 62; sister diagnosed with small cell lung cancer at 40.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking quantified in pack-years (a pack a day since 15, 50 pack-years), chain smoking when stressed, time to first cigarette and previous quit attempts.
kids.d: Critical element: the pack-years. Time to first cigarette and quit attempts are supporting.

kids.x: Alcohol: 5 to 7 standard drinks on special occasions.
Function and support: retired teacher, lives with her husband, well supported, used to walk daily.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: worried her heart is failing or that this is early lung cancer like her sister's; wants to get back to walking.
Examination
Requests vital signs including SpO2, weight and height, and notes SpO2 94% on room air with otherwise normal observations.
check.d: Critical element: requesting SpO2 and noting 94% on room air. Weight and height are supporting.

check.x: General inspection and hands: work of breathing, pursed-lip breathing, accessory muscles, cyanosis; clubbing (absent), nicotine staining, flap.
Neck: tracheal position, JVP (not raised), cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes (none).
Examines the chest front and back and finds signs of hyperinflation and airflow obstruction:

kids.x: Inspection and expansion: barrel-shaped chest, reduced but symmetrical expansion.
Percussion: hyper-resonant throughout with reduced cardiac dullness.
Auscultation: reduced breath sounds, prolonged expiration and scattered expiratory wheeze; no fine crackles.

check.x: Cardiovascular and legs: heart sounds, peripheral and sacral oedema (none), calves.
Interpretation

Observations: SpO2 94% on room air at rest with normal vital signs, falling to 91% with HR 104 and RR 24 after walking and recovering at rest. States she is stable and can be managed in general practice.
Spirometry:

kids.x: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50 (below 0.7 and below the lower limit of normal): persistent airflow limitation, which confirms COPD in this setting.
kids.d: Must state that the ratio is post-bronchodilator and below 0.7 (or the LLN).

kids.x: FEV1 58% predicted: moderate COPD (COPD-X: moderate is 40 to 59%).
No significant bronchodilator response (FEV1 up 60 mL, 5%), which argues against asthma.

check.x: Chest X-ray: hyperinflated lungs with flattened hemidiaphragms, consistent with COPD; no mass, hilar enlargement, consolidation or interstitial change; normal heart size with no congestion. States this is reassuring but does not completely exclude lung cancer.
check.d: Critical element: hyperinflation, and no mass or features of heart failure. Accept the read in the ISBAR assessment or the diagnosis answer.

check.x: Bloods: no anaemia or polycythaemia, normal CRP and renal function (stable, not infected); HbA1c 55 mmol/mol just above target.
check.d: Supporting, not required: eosinophils 0.20 × 10^9/L as a baseline (intermediate; ICS benefit greatest at 0.3 or above, little below 0.1); prednisolone may raise her glucose (credited in item 36).

check.x: States the diagnosis is COPD of moderate severity, justified by 50 pack-years, progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic productive cough, wheeze, flare-ups with colds, hyperinflation on examination and persistent airflow limitation on spirometry.

Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature against: lung cancer (no weight loss, haemoptysis or systemic symptoms, no mass on X-ray), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (productive cough, no crackles or clubbing, obstructive spirometry), heart failure or angina (no orthopnoea, PND or oedema, normal JVP and heart size, tightness comes with wheeze, but still needs an ECG and cardiovascular risk assessment), others such as asthma, TB or atypical pneumonia.
check.d: Source marking: 3 marks, one for each justified differential. Credit any three.

check.x: Management

Explains COPD in plain words (long-term damage and narrowing of the airways from smoking; not curable but treatable, and stopping smoking slows it down) and answers her heart and cancer worries honestly, arranging an ECG/heart-risk check: no sign of heart failure on examination or X-ray; an ECG and heart-risk check because of her diabetes and smoking; no lump on the X-ray, without promising that cancer is impossible.
check.d: Critical element: explains COPD in plain words and answers her heart and cancer worries honestly, arranging an ECG/heart-risk check. Supporting: checks her understanding and invites questions. Do not credit a flat reassurance that it is not her heart without arranging an ECG or a cardiovascular risk check.

check.x: Smoking cessation:

kids.x: Advises clearly that stopping smoking is the most important treatment, asks about her readiness, and offers to set a quit date.
Offers pharmacotherapy (varenicline or combination NRT) and Quitline (13 7848) with follow-up.
kids.d: Supporting: plans for her triggers (other ways to manage stress and the times she chain smokes).

check.x: Refers to pulmonary rehabilitation and encourages regular physical activity.
check.d: Critical element: refers to pulmonary rehabilitation and encourages regular activity. Supporting: about 30 minutes a day; explains that feeling breathless during exercise is expected and safe, and that exercise rebuilds fitness lost to deconditioning. Also supporting: diet and alcohol (her 5 to 7 drinks on special occasions exceeds the 4-a-day limit).

check.x: Recommends annual influenza and pneumococcal vaccination.
check.d: Supporting: COVID-19 and RSV (recommended at her age with lung disease).

check.x: Inhalers: salbutamol 100 micrograms per puff, 2 to 4 puffs as needed as a reliever (for the GP to prescribe), explained in plain words, via a spacer (technique to be taught and checked) and taken as prescribed; starts (preferred) or plans a long-acting bronchodilator (LAMA, stepping up to LAMA/LABA) for her persistent breathlessness; inhaled corticosteroid only for repeated flare-ups despite long-acting bronchodilators (not indicated now).
check.d: Critical element: as-needed reliever via spacer plus a long-acting bronchodilator started or planned. Starting the LAMA now is preferred because her breathlessness persists and limits her activity; credit planning it for the first review. Also credit starting a LAMA/LABA combination (PBS criteria generally require persistent symptoms on monotherapy first).

check.x: Safety netting

Gives a written COPD action plan with a flare-up pack (prednisolone and an antibiotic as prescribed) to keep at home, explains when to start it, and warns prednisolone can raise her blood glucose; arrange a meter or a glucose check with the GP during a course.
check.d: Critical element: the action plan and flare-up pack. The glucose warning is supporting.

check.x: Gives the signs of a flare-up in plain words (more breathless or less able to do her usual activities, more cough or sputum, a change in sputum colour, fever) with the action: start the action plan and see the GP the same day, and go to hospital if not improving or if worried. Call 000 for severe breathlessness at rest, being unable to speak in sentences, blue lips, chest pain or confusion.
check.d: Source: 'if worried, it is always safer to present'. Critical element: the flare-up signs and the 000 triggers, each with an action. Supporting: also see the GP promptly for blood in the phlegm, weight loss or a hoarse voice.

check.x: Arranges GP review in 2 to 4 weeks, and an ECG and AusCVDRisk assessment if not already given in item 30.
check.d: Critical element: GP review in 2 to 4 weeks. The ECG and AusCVDRisk assessment are scored once only (item 30 or here). Desirable, not required: review after every flare-up, repeat spirometry, a statin (likely indicated with diabetes, age 65 and smoking), a GP chronic disease management plan, and discussing CT or the National Lung Cancer Screening Program.

part2.lead: Phoebe had spirometry, a chest X-ray and blood tests during the week and has come back to discuss them. Here are the observations the practice nurse took at her first visit, her spirometry report, her chest X-ray report and her blood results.
part2.patient:
Phoebe is present for questions 3 and 4. While the candidate explains, she asks, if not already covered:

  • "So it's not my heart? And there's no cancer?"
  • "Do I really have to stop smoking completely? It's the only thing that calms me down."

She is relieved to hear there is no sign of heart failure and no lump on the X-ray, but stays anxious because of her sister; she settles with an honest answer and a plan for follow-up. She agrees to set a quit date if the candidate offers real support (medication, Quitline). If the candidate uses jargon ("FEV1", "LAMA") without explaining it, she asks what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse at the first visit, on room air throughout. The 10:25 set was taken straight after Phoebe walked up one flight of stairs and back. Weight 72 kg, height 163 cm (BMI 27).
handover.model:
Read: at rest at 10:10 and 10:40, HR 86 to 88 regular, BP 134 to 136/80 to 82, RR 18, temperature 36.7 °C and alert, with SpO2 94% on room air. After a flight of stairs, SpO2 fell to 91%, HR rose to 104, RR to 24 and BP to 144/84, with mild distress, and all recovered with rest. No hospital observation chart applies in general practice, so judge these against normal adult values.

For Phoebe: her exertional breathlessness is real and objective, with desaturation on exertion, but at rest she is stable and afebrile, with a mildly reduced resting SpO2 (94%), not at a level that needs oxygen assessment. Nothing suggests an acute flare-up or infection today.

What it changes: she can be managed in general practice. COPD-X: consider arterial blood gases and an oxygen assessment if resting SpO2 is 92% or less.

rows.note: Straight after walking up one flight of stairs and back

handover.label: Spirometry report
handover.result:
Examination: spirometry before and after bronchodilator, performed by a respiratory scientist at the community respiratory function laboratory. Phoebe Hartley, 65-year-old woman. Height 163 cm, weight 72 kg. Reference equations: GLI-2012.

Clinical details: progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic productive cough, wheeze. Current smoker, 50 pack-years.

Technique: three acceptable and repeatable manoeuvres before and after salbutamol 400 micrograms via spacer (post-bronchodilator test at 15 minutes). Good effort and cooperation.

MeasurePredictedLLNPre% predictedPost% predictedChange
FEV1 (L)2.241.681.2455%1.3058%+60 mL (+5%)
FVC (L)2.862.202.5589%2.6091%+50 mL (+2%)
FEV1/FVC0.780.670.490.50

Interpretation: the post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio is reduced (0.50, below 0.7 and below the lower limit of normal), indicating airflow obstruction. FEV1 is reduced at 58% predicted. FVC is within normal limits. There is no significant bronchodilator response.

Conclusion: moderate obstructive ventilatory defect without significant bronchodilator reversibility. Consistent with COPD in the appropriate clinical context.
handover.model:
Read: good-quality test. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50, below 0.7 and below the LLN: airflow obstruction that persists after bronchodilator. FEV1 1.30 L, 58% predicted. FVC normal (91%), so no restrictive pattern. FEV1 rose by only 60 mL (5%), which is not a significant bronchodilator response (threshold ≥12% and ≥200 mL, or >10% of predicted value under 2022 ERS/ATS criteria; she meets neither).

For Phoebe: persistent airflow limitation in a 65-year-old with 50 pack-years and typical symptoms confirms COPD. By COPD-X, an FEV1 of 40 to 59% predicted is moderate COPD. The lack of reversibility argues against asthma, and the normal FVC argues against pulmonary fibrosis.

What it changes: this is the confirmed diagnosis that management, PBS-listed long-acting bronchodilators and pulmonary rehabilitation are built on. It is also her baseline for monitoring decline.

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA and lateral, erect. Phoebe Hartley, 65.

Clinical details: progressive exertional breathlessness over months, chronic cough with white sputum, wheeze. Current smoker, 50 pack-years. Sister had lung cancer. Query COPD, query mass.

Comparison: no previous imaging available.

Technique: good inspiration, not rotated, adequately exposed.

Findings:

  • Lungs: hyperinflated, with 7 anterior ribs and 11 posterior ribs visible above the right hemidiaphragm at mid-clavicular line. Mild hyperlucency of both upper zones with attenuated vascular markings. No mass or nodule. No consolidation, cavitation or interstitial (reticular) change.
  • Diaphragm: both hemidiaphragms flattened. Increased retrosternal airspace on the lateral view. Costophrenic angles clear.
  • Hila and mediastinum: hila of normal size and position, with no hilar mass or lymphadenopathy. Mediastinum not widened. Trachea central.
  • Heart: narrow, vertical heart; cardiothoracic ratio 0.42. No upper lobe venous diversion, Kerley B lines or pulmonary oedema.
  • Pleura: no effusion, no pneumothorax.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no rib or bony lesion.
  • Lines and devices: none.

Conclusion: hyperinflated lungs with flattened hemidiaphragms, in keeping with COPD with emphysematous change. No focal mass, consolidation or interstitial change, and no features of cardiac failure. Plain radiography may miss small or central lung lesions; CT is more sensitive if clinically indicated.
handover.model:
Read: correct patient, PA and lateral, adequate film. The key finding is hyperinflation: more than 6 anterior ribs above the diaphragm, flattened hemidiaphragms, increased retrosternal airspace, and a narrow vertical heart, with upper zone hyperlucency. No mass, nodule, hilar enlargement, consolidation or reticular change. Heart size normal, no congestion or effusion. Bones normal.

For Phoebe: this supports COPD with emphysema. A normal heart size with no congestion or effusion is reassuring about heart failure, though a normal film does not exclude heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and the absence of reticular change argues against pulmonary fibrosis. No visible mass is reassuring, but a plain film does not exclude early lung cancer in a 50 pack-year smoker with a family history.

What it changes: no urgent CT is needed for a mass, but keep a low threshold for CT if red flags develop, and CT if the change in cough persists despite COPD treatment; discuss her lung cancer risk at follow-up.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected at the collection centre during the week. No haemolysis.
handover.model:
Read: haemoglobin 141 g/L and the full blood count are normal, with eosinophils 0.20 × 10^9/L. Electrolytes, urea, creatinine (eGFR 88) and CRP are normal. HbA1c 55 mmol/mol (7.2%) is above the laboratory reference range and just above the usual target for type 2 diabetes (53 mmol/mol, 7.0%).

For Phoebe: there is no anaemia to explain her fatigue or breathlessness and no secondary polycythaemia from chronic hypoxia. A normal CRP and white cell count fit stable disease rather than an infection. Eosinophils 0.20 × 10^9/L is an intermediate baseline: inhaled corticosteroid benefit increases with the eosinophil count (little below 0.1, some at 0.1 to 0.3, most at 0.3 or above), which helps decide later whether one is likely to help if flare-ups keep happening despite long-acting bronchodilators.

What it changes: prednisolone in a flare-up pack can raise her blood glucose; arrange a meter or a glucose check with the GP during a course. Her diabetes control should be reviewed (and smoking makes it harder). Her renal function is fine for her metformin.

rows.n: target ≤53 mmol/mol for most adults with type 2 diabetes

ask: Your supervising GP has come back into the room. Please give an ISBAR handover of Phoebe, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Phoebe has come back in. Outline your management of Phoebe now, here in general practice, explaining it to her as you go.
Before Phoebe goes home, what warning signs would you tell her about, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year medical student. Phoebe Hartley, 65, retired teacher.
  • Situation: months of progressive exertional breathlessness and chronic productive cough; spirometry confirms moderate COPD.
  • Background: current smoker, 50 pack-years. Three flare-ups with colds in the last year, no admissions. Type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol; metformin, sitagliptin; no allergies. Sister had small cell lung cancer at 40.
  • Assessment: SpO2 94% at rest, 91% on exertion; stable at rest, suitable for GP management; hyperinflated chest with wheeze. Spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50, FEV1 58% predicted, not reversible: moderate COPD. CXR: hyperinflation, no mass, normal heart. Bloods: no anaemia or polycythaemia, normal CRP and renal function; HbA1c 55, just above target.
  • Recommendation: start COPD management (quit support, reliever via spacer and a LAMA, pulmonary rehab, vaccines, action plan); ECG and cardiovascular risk assessment; review in 2–4 weeks. Please review her and sign the scripts.

Most likely: COPD, moderate severity. For it: 50 pack-years, progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic productive cough, wheeze, fatigue, flare-ups with colds, hyperinflation, persistent airflow limitation (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50).

  • Lung cancer: age, smoking, sister's lung cancer. Against: no weight loss, haemoptysis or systemic symptoms, no mass on X-ray (which does not exclude it).
  • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: progressive breathlessness and fatigue. Against: productive cough, no crackles or clubbing, obstructive not restrictive spirometry.
  • Heart failure or angina: vascular risk factors. Against: no orthopnoea, PND or oedema, normal JVP and heart size; tightness comes with wheeze; needs a 12-lead ECG and absolute CVD risk assessment; BNP or echo if doubt remains.
  • Others: asthma (no reversibility), TB or atypical pneumonia (no fever, sweats or consolidation).

1. Explain: COPD in plain words; no sign of heart failure on examination or X-ray and no lump, but an ECG and heart-risk check because of her diabetes and smoking.
  2. Stopping smoking is the most important step: quit date, varenicline or combination NRT, Quitline 13 7848.
  3. Pulmonary rehabilitation referral and daily activity.
  4. Vaccines: influenza and pneumococcal (COVID-19 and RSV as a bonus).
  5. Inhalers: salbutamol as needed via a spacer; start a LAMA now; no inhaled corticosteroid now.

• Action plan: written action plan and flare-up pack (prednisolone, antibiotic); glucose checks on prednisolone.
  • Flare-up signs: more breathless or less able to do usual things, more cough or phlegm, a change in phlegm colour, fever: start the action plan and see the GP the same day; go to hospital if not improving or worried.
  • Call 000: severe breathlessness at rest, unable to speak in sentences, blue lips, chest pain or confusion.
  • Follow-up: GP in 2 to 4 weeks; ECG and AusCVDRisk.

ddx.for: 50 pack-years, progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic white productive cough, wheeze, flare-ups with colds, hyperinflation with wheeze, and post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50 with FEV1 58% predicted.
Age 65, 50 pack-years, chronic cough, fatigue, and a sister with small cell lung cancer at 40.
ddx.against: No weight loss, appetite change, night sweats, haemoptysis, hoarseness or lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar enlargement on the chest X-ray.

ddx.for: Progressive exertional breathlessness and fatigue in an older smoker.
ddx.against: Productive rather than dry cough, no fine crackles or clubbing, no interstitial change on X-ray, and obstructive rather than restrictive spirometry.

ddx.for: Exertional breathlessness with diabetes, high cholesterol and smoking, and her own worry about her heart.
ddx.against: No orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling or pink frothy sputum, JVP not raised, and a normal heart size with no congestion on X-ray.

ddx.for: Exertional chest tightness that settles with rest in a smoker with diabetes and high cholesterol.
ddx.against: The tightness comes with wheeze and breathlessness, is not crushing, does not radiate and has no sweating or nausea.
No fever, night sweats, weight loss, travel or TB contact, white sputum, normal CRP and no consolidation or cavitation on X-ray.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. The source gives only "Phoebe"; the surname, the morning pattern of the cough, the details of her quit attempts and time to first cigarette, the one course of antibiotics and her vaccination status are added for realism and are consistent with the source. The source marks the history out of 12 (presenting complaint 4, systems review and exclusions 4, past history, medications, family history and social history 1 each); items 5 to 15 follow this.

In Part 2, hand over all four results together and ask the four questions in order. Phoebe is present for questions 3 and 4 and asks her questions if the candidate has not covered them. The source's management task (5 marks) is explained to the patient and follows the SNAPVF structure (Smoking, Nutrition, Alcohol, Physical activity, Vaccinations, plus inhalers); the written action plan is asked for in question 4 alongside the flare-up signs. Credit items 30 to 34 and item 36 whether they come up in question 3 or 4. Credit the X-ray and spirometry reads in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer. Score the ECG and cardiovascular risk assessment once only, in item 30 or item 38. Starting a long-acting bronchodilator (LAMA) now is preferred because her breathlessness persists and limits her activity; accept planning it for the first review, or starting a LAMA/LABA combination.

A high-performing candidate quantifies the decline in exercise tolerance, characterises the sputum, picks up the flare-ups with colds, quantifies the 50 pack-years, screens heart failure, angina, fibrosis and cancer red flags, and draws out her fears. They find hyperinflation and wheeze on examination. In Part 2 they confirm COPD on post-bronchodilator spirometry, grade it as moderate, answer her worries honestly while arranging an ECG and cardiovascular risk assessment, and give a structured plan led by smoking cessation with pharmacotherapy, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, a reliever via spacer with a LAMA started, and a written action plan, with clear red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history without pack-years or exercise tolerance, diagnoses COPD from the X-ray alone, gives a puffer without a spacer or explanation, tells her it is not her heart without arranging an ECG or risk check, says "you should stop smoking" without offering support, or closes with "come back if you're worried".
explain:
Diagnosis: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, moderate

Phoebe is 65 with a 50 pack-year smoking history. She has months of progressive exertional breathlessness (from an hour of hill walking to breathlessness within a kilometre), a chronic cough with white sputum, wheeze, chest tightness, fatigue and three flare-ups with colds in the past year. She has signs of hyperinflation and airflow obstruction. COPD-X requires spirometry to confirm the diagnosis: a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 shows persistent airflow limitation. Hers is 0.50. Severity by COPD-X is graded on FEV1 % predicted together with symptoms: mild 60 to 80%, moderate 40 to 59%, severe below 40%. Her FEV1 of 58% predicted with breathlessness limiting her daily activity is moderate COPD.

The dyspnoea history

  • Breathlessness: onset, progression, exercise tolerance quantified then and now, triggers, recovery, and impact on daily life.
  • Cough and sputum: duration, colour (a change to green, yellow or brown suggests an infective flare), volume and blood.
  • Flare-ups: how many in the last year, how they were treated, and any hospital admissions. These guide the choice of inhaler.
  • Exclusions: heart failure (orthopnoea, PND, oedema, pink frothy sputum), angina (character of the chest tightness), pulmonary fibrosis (dry cough, exposures), lung cancer (weight loss, haemoptysis, night sweats, hoarseness, nodes) and infection or TB.
  • Smoking: pack-years (packs per day multiplied by years smoked), time to first cigarette (within 30 minutes suggests high nicotine dependence), previous quit attempts and triggers.

The differentials

  • Lung cancer: her age, smoking and sister's lung cancer all raise the risk, and COPD itself increases it. No weight loss, haemoptysis or mass is reassuring, but a plain X-ray does not exclude early lung cancer. Her age (50 to 70) and smoking history (at least 30 pack-years, currently smoking) meet the criteria for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program's 2-yearly low-dose CT, which is for people without symptoms suggesting lung cancer; any red flag needs diagnostic investigation instead.
  • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: typically a dry cough, fine "velcro" basal crackles, clubbing, reticular change on imaging and a restrictive pattern. Her productive cough and obstructive spirometry argue against it.
  • Heart failure and angina: her worry, and she has diabetes, smoking and high cholesterol. There is no orthopnoea, PND or oedema, the JVP and heart size are normal, and her chest tightness behaves like airway tightness. The history alone cannot exclude ischaemia, though: women and people with diabetes often present atypically, and a normal chest X-ray does not exclude heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Arrange a 12-lead ECG and an absolute cardiovascular risk assessment (AusCVDRisk), with BNP or echocardiography if doubt remains. A statin is likely indicated given her diabetes, age and smoking.
  • Asthma: can coexist with COPD. A large bronchodilator response, atopy or variable symptoms would suggest it; she has none.
  • TB and atypical pneumonia: no fever, sweats, weight loss, travel or consolidation.

Interpreting the results

  • Spirometry: check quality, then the post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC (obstruction), FEV1 % predicted (severity), FVC (restriction) and the bronchodilator response.
  • Chest X-ray: hyperinflation (more than 6 anterior ribs above the diaphragm, flat hemidiaphragms, increased retrosternal airspace, narrow heart). It excludes other causes (mass, heart failure, fibrosis, consolidation) but cannot diagnose COPD on its own.
  • Observations: desaturation on exertion with a resting SpO2 of 94%. COPD-X: consider arterial blood gases and an oxygen assessment if resting SpO2 is 92% or less.
  • Bloods: exclude anaemia and polycythaemia; the eosinophil count helps predict benefit from inhaled corticosteroid; HbA1c matters because prednisolone raises blood glucose.

Management (COPD-X and Lung Foundation Australia): SNAPVF

  • Smoking: stopping is the single most effective intervention to slow decline. Ask, advise and help: set a quit date, offer pharmacotherapy (varenicline, combination nicotine replacement therapy, or bupropion), refer to Quitline (13 7848), plan for stress triggers, and book follow-up. Relapse is common; keep offering support.
  • Nutrition: a healthy diet and a dietitian referral where needed.
  • Alcohol: NHMRC guidance is no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day. Her 5 to 7 drinks on special occasions exceeds the daily limit.
  • Physical activity: pulmonary rehabilitation (supervised exercise training and education, usually over about 8 weeks) improves breathlessness, exercise capacity and quality of life. Aim for 30 minutes of activity a day. Breathlessness during exercise is expected and safe, and exercise counters deconditioning.
  • Vaccinations: annual influenza, pneumococcal vaccination (COPD is a risk condition) and COVID-19 according to the Australian Immunisation Handbook; RSV vaccine is recommended for adults aged 60 to 74 with chronic lung disease. Avoid sick contacts.
  • Inhalers (stepwise): a short-acting bronchodilator (salbutamol 200 to 400 micrograms, 2 to 4 puffs via a spacer) as needed for everyone. For persistent breathlessness, add a long-acting bronchodilator (a LAMA such as tiotropium, or a LABA), then a LAMA/LABA combination. With persistent breathlessness limiting daily activity, start a LAMA now rather than relying on a reliever alone. An inhaled corticosteroid is added (as triple therapy) for repeated flare-ups despite long-acting bronchodilators; a higher blood eosinophil count predicts more benefit. Inhaled corticosteroid alone is not used in COPD.
  • Inhaler technique and adherence: check at every visit. Spacer: assemble, shake the puffer, attach, breathe out, seal lips around the mouthpiece, press once, take 4 normal breaths in and out; shake again and repeat for each puff.
  • COPD action plan: a written plan with a flare-up pack kept at home. eTG and COPD-X: prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally once daily for 5 days; an antibiotic when the sputum becomes purulent (amoxicillin 500 mg orally 8-hourly for 5 days, or doxycycline 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg daily for 4 days). With diabetes, prednisolone can raise her blood glucose; she is on metformin and sitagliptin and may not have a meter, so arrange a meter or a glucose check with the GP during a course.

Safety netting and follow-up

Teach the signs of a flare-up: more breathless or less able to do usual things, more cough or sputum, a change in sputum colour, or fever. She should start the action plan and see the GP the same day, and go to hospital if not improving; if worried, it is always safer to present. Call 000 for severe breathlessness at rest, being unable to speak in sentences, blue lips, chest pain or confusion. See the GP promptly for coughing up blood, weight loss, a hoarse voice, new lumps, or a cough that keeps changing or doesn't settle with treatment. Review in 2 to 4 weeks for smoking, inhaler technique and symptoms; arrange an ECG and an AusCVDRisk assessment; review after every flare-up (a flare-up is also a prompt to refer to pulmonary rehabilitation); and review regularly with repeat spirometry. A GP chronic disease management plan supports allied health input.

More on management

  • Smoking cessation also needs stress strategies and follow-up.
  • Inhaler technique and adherence are checked at every visit; if breathlessness persists on a LAMA, step up to LAMA/LABA.
  • Diet and alcohol: no more than 4 standard drinks on any day and 10 a week (NHMRC).

Follow-up and lung cancer

Review after every flare-up and repeat spirometry regularly. A statin is likely indicated with diabetes, age 65 and smoking. A chronic disease management plan brings in a dietitian and exercise physiology. Given her smoking history, discuss the National Lung Cancer Screening Program, and see the GP promptly for coughing up blood, weight loss, a hoarse voice, new lumps or a cough that keeps changing.
points: COPD is confirmed on spirometry by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7; by COPD-X, an FEV1 of 40 to 59% predicted is moderate disease. A chest X-ray supports it and excludes other causes but cannot diagnose it.

In exertional breathlessness, quantify the exercise tolerance and its decline, the flare-ups in the last year and the pack-years, and screen for heart failure, angina, pulmonary fibrosis and lung cancer red flags. In a woman with diabetes who smokes, a reassuring history does not exclude ischaemia: arrange an ECG and absolute cardiovascular risk assessment.
Stopping smoking is the most effective treatment: set a quit date, offer varenicline or combination nicotine replacement, refer to Quitline (13 7848) and follow up.
Use SNAPVF to structure the plan: Smoking, Nutrition, Alcohol, Physical activity (pulmonary rehabilitation), Vaccinations, plus inhalers and a written action plan.

Inhalers step up from a reliever via spacer to a LAMA, then LAMA/LABA; with persistent breathlessness limiting activity, start the LAMA now. Add an inhaled corticosteroid only for repeated flare-ups. Teach and check spacer technique at every visit.

A flare-up pack (prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days, with an antibiotic for purulent sputum) can raise blood glucose in a patient with diabetes, so arrange a meter or a glucose check with the GP during a course.
